screens.title: Redis Sentinel: Automated Failover and Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore Redis Sentinel, the lightweight distributed system Redis provides to monitor instances and automate failover. You will learn why Sentinel exists, how multiple Sentinel processes cooperate to avoid single points of failure, and how clients discover the current master so applications can continue without manual reconfiguration. We'll ground the ideas with concrete configuration lines from sentinel. conf and a simple lab that runs three Sentinels watching a master and two replicas. As we go, notice two critical notions: quorum, which prevents a single Sentinel from making a unilateral decision, and the distinction between a Sentinel’s subjective view and the objective consensus that triggers failover. You will see the failover steps a leader performs: selecting the best replica, promoting it, reconfiguring replicas, and informing clients. By the end you'll understand common pitfalls — like running only one Sentinel or blocking Sentinel ports with a firewall — and how to choose appropriate timeouts for your environment. Keep in mind that Sentinel is supervisory, not a data replication mechanism; it works with replication to provide high availability.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Redis Sentinel

Redis Sentinel: Automated Failover and Monitoring

Understand how Sentinel supervises Redis, elects leaders, and performs failover with quorum to keep services available.

In this lesson
Sentinel roles, failover steps, and client discovery.
Hands-on
Start three Sentinels, run SENTINEL masters, simulate SHUTDOWN, observe sdown → odown → promotion.
Key focus
Quorum, leader election, and safe promotion rules.
Explore Key Topics
Monitoring
How Sentinels check master and replica health and mark SDOWN.
Failover
Quorum, leader election, promotion steps and notifying clients.
Client Discovery
Clients ask Sentinels for the current master rather than hardcoding IPs.
Architecture snapshot
Multiple Sentinels supervise a master and replicas to avoid a single point of failure.
Master: 127.0.0.1:6379
Replica A: 127.0.0.1:6380
Replica B: 127.0.0.1:6381
Sentinels: 26379, 26380, 26381 — quorum 2
Key takeaway
Sentinel turns replication into a highly available system by monitoring, voting, and promoting replicas when needed.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the purpose and architecture of Redis Sentinel, configure a basic Sentinel setup, and reason about its automatic failover process. You will be able to run multiple Sentinel processes to eliminate single points of failure, read the sentinel. conf parameters that control monitoring and timeouts, and simulate a controlled failover in a lab. You will also learn how clients discover the current master through Sentinel queries rather than hardcoded IPs, and why that matters for resilient applications. Finally, you will understand quorum and majority voting: how Sentinels avoid split-brain by requiring an agreed number of votes before acting. Each objective pairs a practical task with a conceptual check so you can both operate Sentinel and explain its safety guarantees. For example, configuring three Sentinels with a quorum of two ensures that if one node dies, the remaining two can still make a correct decision. Keep this outcome-focused view in mind as you follow the hands-on steps and diagnostics in the lessons ahead.

screens.title: What is Redis Sentinel?
screens.narratorSegment: Redis Sentinel is a supervision system that sits alongside Redis replication and provides monitoring, notifications, and automatic failover. It does not replicate data itself. Instead, Sentinel watches the health of a master and its replicas. If the master becomes unreachable, Sentinels collaborate to determine whether the master is truly down and, if so, promote a replica to become the new master. This makes Sentinel complementary to replication: replication handles data redundancy and read scaling, while Sentinel handles availability. A common misconception is to think Sentinel replaces backups or replication; it does not. Another misconception is that a single Sentinel can provide high availability; it cannot because it would itself be a single point of failure. Practically, you run multiple Sentinel processes on separate hosts and configure a quorum so that several Sentinels must agree before failover. For example, with three Sentinels and a quorum of two, a single network glitch or Sentinel crash cannot trigger a promotion. Remember that Sentinel provides client discovery too — clients query Sentinel to obtain the current master's address so they can reconnect after a failover without manual updates. What matters is combining replication for data and Sentinel for orchestration.

keyIdea.title: Sentinel = supervision, not replication
keyIdea.text: Sentinel monitors and orchestrates failover while replication provides the data copies that become the promoted master.

content.html:
Core Concept › Definition › What is Redis Sentinel?
Definition
Sentinel is a distributed supervisor that monitors Redis instances, issues notifications, elects leaders, and performs automatic failover when necessary.
Monitoring: check master and replicas for reachability
Notification: emit events when state changes
Automatic Failover: elect leader and promote replica
Common misconception
Sentinel does not replace replication or backups. It supervises failover but depends on replicas for data continuity.
Concrete example
You run one master on port 6379 and two replicas on 6380 and 6381. Three Sentinel processes monitor the master. If the master stops responding, at least two Sentinels must agree before a promotion occurs.
Key Takeaway

Use Sentinel to supervise replication and orchestrate failover; it increases availability but does not change how data is replicated.

screens.title: Sentinel topology and deployment patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Sentinel is intentionally distributed. Each Sentinel process runs independently and communicates with other Sentinels and Redis instances. The recommended deployment is at least three Sentinels running on separate hosts so that the monitoring service itself is highly available. Using an odd number of Sentinels simplifies majority calculations: with three Sentinels and a quorum of two, the system can tolerate the failure of one Sentinel and still reach a decision. If your deployment had only two Sentinels and one fails, the remaining Sentinel could not reach a quorum of two and failovers would be blocked. A common operational error is to run both Sentinels and Redis on the same physical machine; this creates correlated failure risk. Another important detail is network connectivity: Sentinels must be able to talk to each other and to each Redis node. Firewalls that block these ports lead to false SDOWN markings or failed leader elections. When placing Sentinels, think about spreading them across availability zones or distinct machines to reduce correlated failures. The overall goal is to make the supervision layer as fault-tolerant as the data layer it manages.

keyIdea.title: Topology matters
keyIdea.text: Run multiple Sentinels across independent hosts and prefer odd counts so quorum and leader election work reliably under failure.

content.html:
Architecture › Topology › Deployment patterns
Topology checklist
  • Deploy at least three Sentinel processes on different hosts.
  • Prefer odd numbers to simplify majority voting.
  • Ensure Sentinels and Redis instances can communicate across firewall rules.
  • Avoid co-locating all Sentinels on a single physical host.
Deployment tips
Spread Sentinels across zones and configure monitoring thresholds appropriate to network latency to avoid flapping promotions.
Scenario
Three Sentinels on separate machines observe a master. One Sentinel's host crashes. Remaining two can still reach quorum and safely elect a leader to perform failover.
Common mistake

Running a single Sentinel defeats the point of high availability for the monitoring system. It creates a single point of failure for failover decisions.

screens.title: Failover life cycle: SDOWN → ODOWN → Election → Promotion
screens.narratorSegment: Failover in Sentinel follows a clear sequence of states and actions. First, a Sentinel can mark a Redis instance as subjectively down, or SDOWN, when it cannot contact the instance for the configured down-after-milliseconds. SDOWN is a single Sentinel's local view and does not trigger failover by itself. If multiple Sentinels also report the same instance as down and the count meets the configured quorum, the instance becomes objectively down, or ODOWN. Once ODOWN is established, Sentinels elect a leader among themselves using a consensus protocol; the elected leader orchestrates the failover. The leader selects the best replica to promote based on replication offset and configured priorities. It then sends the command to promote that replica to master, reconfigures other replicas to follow the new master, updates its own configuration state, and notifies clients. A misconception is that failover is instantaneous; in reality there are timeout windows and safety checks to avoid split-brain and to ensure promotion only happens when appropriate. Practically, tuning down-after-milliseconds and failover-timeout balances sensitivity and stability for your environment. Failover life cycle: SDOWN → ODOWN → Election → Promotion means sentinels progress from sdown to odown, then elect a leader to promote a replica while minimizing split-brain risk.. In practical terms, step-by-step orchestration performed by sentinels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ordered safety checks
keyIdea.text: Sentinels progress from SDOWN to ODOWN, then elect a leader to promote a replica while minimizing split-brain risk.

content.html:
Process Flow › Failover life cycle › SDOWN to Promotion
Step sequence
  1. Sentinel marks SDOWN after down-after-milliseconds.
  2. Other Sentinels report similar SDOWN; quorum reached → ODOWN.
  3. Sentinels elect a leader to coordinate failover.
  4. Leader selects best replica and promotes it with REPLICAOF NO ONE.
  5. Leader reconfigures remaining replicas to follow the new master.
  6. Clients are informed and reconnect to the new master.
Pro tip
Configure parallel-syncs and replication priorities so the chosen replica is ready to be promoted with minimal data loss risk.
Concrete example
A master at 6379 stops responding. After 5 seconds a Sentinel marks SDOWN. Two Sentinels report SDOWN, meeting quorum=2, so the state becomes ODOWN. A leader is elected and promotes replica at 6380, then updates other replicas to follow 6380.
Key Takeaway

Failover is a coordinated multi-Sentinel decision, designed to reduce mistakes by requiring multiple confirmations and a leader to act.

screens.title: Minimal sentinel.conf explained
screens.narratorSegment: The sentinel. conf file directs a Sentinel process what to monitor and how to behave. A minimal example includes port, logging, and the sentinel monitor line that names the monitored master and the quorum. The monitor line has the form sentinel monitor ; the final number is the number of Sentinels required to agree before a failover can be initiated. Other important parameters are down-after-milliseconds, which controls how long a Sentinel waits before marking SDOWN, and failover-timeout, which bounds how long the failover may take. Parallel-syncs controls how many replicas are allowed to re-sync in parallel during failover. In practice, you'll copy the example three times with different ports for each Sentinel process. A common pitfall is copying the same pidfile or logfile into different Sentinels; give each instance unique files. It's also important to ensure Sentinels run on distinct hosts where possible. In lab steps we start three sentinel processes with their own configs and observe their cooperative behavior. Minimal sentinel.conf explained means use sentinel monitor to set names and quorum; tune down-after-milliseconds and failover-timeout to balance promptness and stability.. In practical terms, key parameters you will edit and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sentinel config essentials
keyIdea.text: Use sentinel monitor to set names and quorum; tune down-after-milliseconds and failover-timeout to balance promptness and stability.

content.html:
Configuration › sentinel.conf › Key parameters
Minimal sentinel.conf
port 26379
daemonize yes
pidfile /var/run/redis-sentinel.pid
logfile "/var/log/redis-sentinel.log"
dir /tmp
sentinel monitor mymaster 127.0.0.1 6379 2
sentinel down-after-milliseconds mymaster 5000
sentinel failover-timeout mymaster 60000
sentinel parallel-syncs mymaster 1
Note the monitor line's last number is the quorum required to trigger failover.
Parameter meanings
  • sentinel monitor: which master to watch and quorum.
  • down-after-milliseconds: time before marking SDOWN.
  • failover-timeout: upper bound for failover operations.
  • parallel-syncs: replicas allowed to resync in parallel.
Practical note

Start each Sentinel with a unique port and unique pid/log files. Use three Sentinels and quorum 2 for laboratory setups.

screens.title: Starting three Sentinels and observing state
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the lab steps to start three Sentinel processes and monitor them. First, ensure your master on 6379 and two replicas on 6380 and 6381 are running. Then create three configuration files sentinel1. conf, sentinel2. conf, sentinel3. conf with identical monitor lines but different ports. Start each Sentinel process with the redis-sentinel command and its config file. After they are running, connect to any Sentinel using redis-cli -p 26379 and run INFO sentinel and SENTINEL masters. INFO sentinel shows connected Sentinels and monitored masters; SENTINEL masters lists each master and its state. You should see a monitored master named mymaster and entries for connected sentinels. If you shutdown the master, the Sentinels will progress through sdown and odown states. Watch SENTINEL masters repeatedly to observe the state changes and eventual elected master address. This is diagnostic practice: reading these outputs helps you understand how sentinel reports its view of the system and confirms that Sentinels communicate correctly. Hands-on › Lab steps › Start Sentinels
Terminal demo commands
# Start Sentinel 1
redis-sentinel sentinel1.conf &
# Start Sentinel 2
redis-sentinel sentinel2.conf &
# Start Sentinel 3
redis-sentinel sentinel3.conf &
# Connect to Sentinel CLI
redis-cli -p 26379
# Inspect sentinel state
INFO sentinel
SENTINEL masters
What to expect
You will see the master listed and connected Sentinels. During a simulated shutdown, states move from sdown to odown and then to a new master address once promotion completes.
Common outputs
SENTINEL masters output contains keys like name, ip, port, flags and number of replicas. Flags show odown or sdown states.
Practice reading the flags to know when promotion is in progress.
Lab tip
Run the SENTINEL masters command in a loop to watch transitions when you shut down the master.

screens.title: Simulating master failure and observing promotion
screens.narratorSegment: In this simulation you will intentionally stop the master and observe how Sentinels react. First connect to the master instance on port 6379 and issue SHUTDOWN. Immediately switch to a Sentinel CLI and run SENTINEL masters in a loop. Initially you will see one or more Sentinels mark the master as subjectively down; the master will appear with an sdown flag. When enough Sentinels report the same issue matching quorum, the master becomes objectively down and the odown flag appears. At that moment a leader election occurs. The elected leader checks replica offsets and priorities, selects the best candidate, sends the command to promote it to master, and reconfigures other replicas to follow. After promotion you will see the master's ip:port entry in SENTINEL masters point to the new master address, for example 127.0.0.1:6380. Then verify by connecting to the new master and running INFO replication to confirm its role. A common misconception is that clients automatically switch instantly; client libraries need to query Sentinel or have built-in Sentinel support to reconnect to the new master. Simulating master failure and observing promotion means shutdown the master, follow sdown → odown, watch leader election, and confirm the new master with info replication.. In practical terms, shutdown the master and follow sentinels through the failover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Sentinel client discovery vs hardcoded masters
screens.narratorSegment: Clients have two common strategies to find the Redis master: hardcoding a master address or querying Sentinel for the current master. Hardcoding is simple but brittle: when a failover happens the application must be manually reconfigured, which leads to downtime. Using Sentinel for discovery is more robust. Clients connect to one or more Sentinel instances and ask for the master's current address for a given service name. When a promotion happens, Sentinels report the new master's address, and client libraries with Sentinel support will reconnect automatically. Another pitfall is listing only one Sentinel address in client configs; it's safer to configure multiple Sentinels so the client can still find the master if one Sentinel is down. Design client code to retry Sentinel queries and to gracefully reconnect to the provided master address. screens.title: Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes teams make when deploying Sentinel. First, running a single Sentinel is a fatal design error: it leaves the monitoring system with a single point of failure and no quorum. Second, misconfigured firewall rules that prevent Sentinels from talking to each other or to Redis instances cause false SDOWN reports or prevent leader elections. Third, using too-small down-after-milliseconds makes Sentinel overly sensitive to transient network issues, producing unnecessary failovers. Fourth, not giving each Sentinel a unique pidfile or logfile can lead to process management confusion. Finally, depending on clients to automatically migrate open connections is a misconception — client libraries must re-query Sentinel and reconnect to the new master. To avoid these issues, deploy at least three Sentinels on separate hosts, validate network connectivity before relying on automated failover, and tune timeouts to your environment. Run simulated failovers in a staging environment to validate the entire chain: Sentinels, election, promotion, replica reconfiguration, and client reconnection. Top mistakes

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the three most important concepts from this chapter so you can carry them into operations. First, Sentinel supervises Redis for availability; it monitors, not replicates. You must pair Sentinels with replication so there is a candidate replica to promote. Second, quorum and majority voting prevent unilateral promotions. Prefer an odd number of Sentinels and set a quorum that matches your deployment size so failovers are safe and possible under realistic node loss. Third, clients should use Sentinel-based discovery to adapt to a new master automatically; they should not rely on hardcoded master addresses. Together, these concepts reduce downtime and make your Redis deployment resilient. A final practice reminder: test failovers in staging, record outputs from SENTINEL masters and INFO sentinel, and tune timeouts before relying on automatic failover in production.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore Redis Sentinel, the lightweight distributed system Redis provides to monitor instances and automate failover. You will learn why Sentinel exists, how multiple Sentinel processes cooperate to avoid single points of failure, and how clients discover the current master so applications can continue without manual reconfiguration. We'll ground the ideas with concrete configuration lines from sentinel. conf and a simple lab that runs three Sentinels watching a master and two replicas. As we go, notice two critical notions: quorum, which prevents a single Sentinel from making a unilateral decision, and the distinction between a Sentinel’s subjective view and the objective consensus that triggers failover. You will see the failover steps a leader performs: selecting the best replica, promoting it, reconfiguring replicas, and informing clients. By the end you'll understand common pitfalls — like running only one Sentinel or blocking Sentinel ports with a firewall — and how to choose appropriate timeouts for your environment. Keep in mind that Sentinel is supervisory, not a data replication mechanism; it works with replication to provide high availability.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the purpose and architecture of Redis Sentinel, configure a basic Sentinel setup, and reason about its automatic failover process. You will be able to run multiple Sentinel processes to eliminate single points of failure, read the sentinel. conf parameters that control monitoring and timeouts, and simulate a controlled failover in a lab. You will also learn how clients discover the current master through Sentinel queries rather than hardcoded IPs, and why that matters for resilient applications. Finally, you will understand quorum and majority voting: how Sentinels avoid split-brain by requiring an agreed number of votes before acting. Each objective pairs a practical task with a conceptual check so you can both operate Sentinel and explain its safety guarantees. For example, configuring three Sentinels with a quorum of two ensures that if one node dies, the remaining two can still make a correct decision. Keep this outcome-focused view in mind as you follow the hands-on steps and diagnostics in the lessons ahead.

This second objectives screen guides the learner to deeper operational checks and design considerations. You will learn to interpret sentinel state outputs such as sdown and odown, and to use SENTINEL masters and INFO sentinel to verify the cluster state. You will practice choosing sensible timeouts like down-after-milliseconds and failover-timeout so that transient network blips don't cause unnecessary promotions. You will also learn to prefer odd numbers of Sentinels to simplify quorum decisions and reduce split-brain risk. Finally, you will identify common misconfigurations: running a single Sentinel, blocking ports, or setting an unrealistic quorum that blocks failovers. Each objective contains a short mnemonic and a competency note to help you prepare for a real environment where availability matters. Practically, after completing the hands-on lab you should be able to start three Sentinel processes, simulate a master shutdown, and watch Sentinels elect a new master and reconfigure replicas with minimal downtime.

Redis Sentinel is a supervision system that sits alongside Redis replication and provides monitoring, notifications, and automatic failover. It does not replicate data itself. Instead, Sentinel watches the health of a master and its replicas. If the master becomes unreachable, Sentinels collaborate to determine whether the master is truly down and, if so, promote a replica to become the new master. This makes Sentinel complementary to replication: replication handles data redundancy and read scaling, while Sentinel handles availability. A common misconception is to think Sentinel replaces backups or replication; it does not. Another misconception is that a single Sentinel can provide high availability; it cannot because it would itself be a single point of failure. Practically, you run multiple Sentinel processes on separate hosts and configure a quorum so that several Sentinels must agree before failover. For example, with three Sentinels and a quorum of two, a single network glitch or Sentinel crash cannot trigger a promotion. Remember that Sentinel provides client discovery too — clients query Sentinel to obtain the current master's address so they can reconnect after a failover without manual updates. What matters is combining replication for data and Sentinel for orchestration.

Sentinel is intentionally distributed. Each Sentinel process runs independently and communicates with other Sentinels and Redis instances. The recommended deployment is at least three Sentinels running on separate hosts so that the monitoring service itself is highly available. Using an odd number of Sentinels simplifies majority calculations: with three Sentinels and a quorum of two, the system can tolerate the failure of one Sentinel and still reach a decision. If your deployment had only two Sentinels and one fails, the remaining Sentinel could not reach a quorum of two and failovers would be blocked. A common operational error is to run both Sentinels and Redis on the same physical machine; this creates correlated failure risk. Another important detail is network connectivity: Sentinels must be able to talk to each other and to each Redis node. Firewalls that block these ports lead to false SDOWN markings or failed leader elections. When placing Sentinels, think about spreading them across availability zones or distinct machines to reduce correlated failures. The overall goal is to make the supervision layer as fault-tolerant as the data layer it manages.

Failover in Sentinel follows a clear sequence of states and actions. First, a Sentinel can mark a Redis instance as subjectively down, or SDOWN, when it cannot contact the instance for the configured down-after-milliseconds. SDOWN is a single Sentinel's local view and does not trigger failover by itself. If multiple Sentinels also report the same instance as down and the count meets the configured quorum, the instance becomes objectively down, or ODOWN. Once ODOWN is established, Sentinels elect a leader among themselves using a consensus protocol; the elected leader orchestrates the failover. The leader selects the best replica to promote based on replication offset and configured priorities. It then sends the command to promote that replica to master, reconfigures other replicas to follow the new master, updates its own configuration state, and notifies clients. A misconception is that failover is instantaneous; in reality there are timeout windows and safety checks to avoid split-brain and to ensure promotion only happens when appropriate. Practically, tuning down-after-milliseconds and failover-timeout balances sensitivity and stability for your environment. Failover life cycle: SDOWN → ODOWN → Election → Promotion means sentinels progress from sdown to odown, then elect a leader to promote a replica while minimizing split-brain risk.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's summarize the three most important concepts from this chapter so you can carry them into operations. First, Sentinel supervises Redis for availability; it monitors, not replicates. You must pair Sentinels with replication so there is a candidate replica to promote. Second, quorum and majority voting prevent unilateral promotions. Prefer an odd number of Sentinels and set a quorum that matches your deployment size so failovers are safe and possible under realistic node loss. Third, clients should use Sentinel-based discovery to adapt to a new master automatically; they should not rely on hardcoded master addresses. Together, these concepts reduce downtime and make your Redis deployment resilient. A final practice reminder: test failovers in staging, record outputs from SENTINEL masters and INFO sentinel, and tune timeouts before relying on automatic failover in production.
